awd_titl_txt: Conference: 2nd SIAM Northern and Central California Sectional Conference (NCC25)
awd_abstract_narration:
The second annual conference of the Northern and Central California Section of SIAM (SIAM-NCC) will be held October 27–28, 2025, at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. This event brings together researchers from academia, industry, national laboratories, and government to strengthen regional collaboration in applied and computational mathematics. The conference aims to: (1) create an opportunity for scientific researchers to meet, network, and share the innovations and recent developments in their fields; (2) attract and energize students and researchers working in applied and computational mathematics and related fields; (3) offer SIAM members from all institutions in the NCC region the opportunity to attend a local meeting of the community; (4) provide early career researchers the access and opportunities to connect with others who are at similar career stages; (5) inspire the next generation of applied and computational mathematicians to get involved in the community and to innovate through research and education.

Conference themes align with SIAM Activity Groups and include mathematical analysis, optimization, inverse problems, experimental design, high-performance computing, uncertainty quantification, scientific machine learning, AI, and digital twins. The program will feature two plenary talks, eight thematic sessions, two panels, two poster sessions with blitz presentations, a mentoring event, a CV/interviewing workshop, and guided tours of the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) and the Advanced Light Source (ALS). The presenters will come from academia, industry, and national laboratories, representing many scientific backgrounds, career stages, and institutional affiliations. The themes and speakers for each thematic session will be selected via an open call and coordinated by the Technical Program Committee. More information is available at the conference: https://siamncc25.lbl.gov.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award supported students and early-career researchers attending the 2nd SIAM Northern and Central California Sectional Conference (NCC25), held October 27–28, 2025, at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) in Berkeley, California. The conference was jointly organized by the University of California, Berkeley, and LBNL. NSF funding provided more than 60 travel awards to students and early-career professionals from across the region. These awards made it possible for many participants to attend who otherwise could not have afforded the trip.

The Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM) is a professional society for people who use mathematics and computing to solve real-world problems in science, engineering, medicine, and industry. In 2024, SIAM established its Northern and Central California (NCC) Section to give researchers in the region, especially students and those early in their careers, a local place to share their work and build professional connections. Many of these researchers cannot easily travel to SIAM's large national and international meetings. The section's first conference took place at UC Merced in October 2024 and drew nearly 200 attendees. NCC25 built on that success.

More than 200 people attended NCC25. They included high school, undergraduate, and graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, university faculty, national laboratory scientists, and industry engineers. Most participants came from Northern California and the Central Valley, but the program also drew presenters and attendees from across the United States.

Intellectual Merit

The scientific program showed how mathematics and computation drive progress across many fields. Two invited plenary lectures anchored the conference. Robert Falgout of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory opened the meeting with an overview of multigrid methods. These techniques allow scientists to solve enormous systems of equations efficiently on the world's most powerful supercomputers, and Falgout described recent advances that let them run on the newest generation of machines. On the second day, Suzanne Sindi of UC Merced showed how mathematical models serve as tools for discovery in biology. Her talk explained how researchers can study living processes that unfold across vastly different scales of size and time, while accounting for uncertainty in what is known.

The program also included 40 contributed talks organized into eight thematic sessions. A Technical Program Committee selected them through an open call for submissions. Committee members came from universities, national laboratories, and companies across the region. Session topics included high-performance computing and simulation, uncertainty quantification and data-driven modeling, machine learning for scientific computing, linear algebra and numerical methods, scientific computing for the life sciences, computational methods for partial differential equations, and control theory and optimization. Talks addressed applications ranging from cloud physics and climate modeling to real-time imaging at X-ray facilities and the coordination of autonomous systems.

Attendees also presented 44 research posters across two interactive poster sessions. Each session was introduced by a "poster blitz," in which every presenter gave a brief summary to the full audience. Students and early-career researchers made up most of the poster presenters, which gave them valuable experience communicating their work. Judges recognized outstanding posters by a variety of presenters.

Broader Impacts

The most direct impact of this award was broader access to the conference. NSF support funded more than 60 travel awards, which covered expenses such as lodging and transportation for students and early-career researchers with limited research funds. These awards were especially important for participants from the Central Valley and more rural parts of the state, where travel to the Bay Area can be costly. The resulting strong local attendance was a highlight for the organizers.

NCC25 also emphasized professional development alongside research. In one panel, leaders from industry, national laboratories, and academia discussed how artificial intelligence and large language models are changing the way research is conducted, reproduced, and shared. A second panel, aimed at more established researchers, focused on challenges in mentoring early-career professionals, including networking and career transitions. At the same time, students and junior scientists took part in an interviewing and resume workshop. An LBNL human resources specialist reviewed interview strategies, and participants then received small-group feedback on their CVs and resumes. Strong participation in both events showed how much attendees valued practical career guidance.

The conference also used its location at a national laboratory to expose attendees to world-class scientific infrastructure. Participants toured the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, home of the Perlmutter supercomputer, and the Advanced Light Source, a facility that produces intense X-ray beams for research in materials, chemistry, biology, and more. For many students, these tours offered a first look at careers in national laboratory research.

By bringing together participants from universities, community and state colleges, national laboratories, and private companies, NCC25 strengthened the regional network of people working in applied mathematics and computational science. It also helped prepare the next generation of researchers to contribute to the nation's scientific and technological workforce.
